title: The Seventh Face of the Die: Barcelona, the Dictionary of Symbols, and the Bronwyn Cycle
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Barcelona, the birth in the Eixample
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the Eixample, on the ninth of April 1916, a son is born to Juan Cirlot and Maria Laporta and given his father's name. No plaque marks the house and no source consulted records the street. Barcelona will keep him for all but a handful of years: one posting to Zaragoza, one journey to Paris, nothing else. Piano lessons, Jesuit Latin, a hand-printed magazine, a rack of medieval swords, and a dictionary of symbols that reaches four languages are all decided inside a few square kilometres of this unrecorded address.
suggested_refs: The Eixample of Barcelona in 1916, the district of his unrecorded birth address

stops.name: Carrer de Casp, the Jesuit schoolroom
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from his age; the sources name the school, not the years
stops.campa: Under the black cassocks of the Society of Jesus on Carrer de Casp the boy takes his first Latin, and with the grammar the gods of Rome and of Egypt. The Jesuits teach him rigour and give him nothing at all of the surrealists he will later devour; those arrive twenty years on, in a borrowed library in a garrison town. He collects names the way other boys collect stamps. Decades later, sorting the religious orders by the ground each of them chose to build on, he will remember which order took the cities.
stops.quote: From religious literature we learn that the Order of St. Bruno preferred precipitous and remote places for their communities; the Benedictines would choose mountain-heights; the Cistercians, pleasant valleys; and the Jesuits of St. Ignatius, the cities.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'Symbolic Analogy,' p. xxxix
suggested_refs: The Jesuit college on Carrer de Casp, Barcelona
sources: Cuadernos Hispanoamericanos, 'Cirlot: el poeta y su mundo'

stops.name: Barcelona, eight years under Fernando Ardevol
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources give eight years of study without fixing their start
stops.campa: The maestro Fernando Ardevol drills him in piano and composition for eight years. The training does not make a composer; it makes an ear. He learns to follow a structure while it is still moving, and to catch a figure coming back altered. Later he will read a myth the way he read a score, tracking the motif beneath its variations. One work of his own reaches a public hall. The rest of the music turns inward and becomes method, the habit of hearing a system where other men hear a story.
suggested_refs: Fernando Ardevol, Barcelona composition teacher of the 1930s
sources: Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes, author-authority record

stops.name: Banco Hispanoamericano, the ledgers
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source dates his years at the customs agency or the bank
stops.campa: Before the war there is a customs agency, then a clerk's desk at the Banco Hispanoamericano and columns that must balance by evening. No source names the branch, and none dates his start at either job. Nothing in the arithmetic predicts a dictionary of symbols, and he never treats the two lives as opposites: a ledger is also a system in which every entry answers another. He goes home to the piano. The decade runs out on schedule, and in July of his twentieth year the war begins.
suggested_refs: The Banco Hispanoamericano in Barcelona, employer before and after the Civil War

stops.name: Barcelona, the war arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1936; the day is context, not record
stops.campa: In July the checkpoints go up and the requisitions begin, and the routines that shaped his twenties end overnight. He is twenty years old. Within a year he will carry a rifle for the Republic; within four, for the men who defeat it. No letter or diary has surfaced in which he explains the passage from one uniform to the other, and no biographer consulted has found one. The city he was born in is at war with itself and he is inside it, holding a pass and waiting to be called.
suggested_refs: Barcelona, July 1936, the first weeks of the Civil War

stops.name: Barcelona, mobilized for the Republic
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month, no unit, no sector recorded in any source consulted
stops.campa: He is mobilized to fight for the Second Spanish Republic. That is the whole of the record: no unit, no sector, no engagement, no letter home. The Aragon front runs through Huesca and Belchite and Teruel in these years and is the likeliest country for him, but nothing places him in it. The man who will spend thirty years cataloguing what a sword means carries a rifle here for a government he is conscripted three years later to fight against, and says nothing about either afterwards.
suggested_refs: The Aragon front, 1937, the likeliest theatre of a service the sources do not describe
sources: gap: no source names his unit or sector

stops.name: Zaragoza, mobilized by the victors
stops.date_confidence: attested to the start of 1940; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: At the start of 1940 he is called up again, this time by the winning side, and posted to Zaragoza for three years. The Basilica del Pilar stands over a city he did not choose. He finds there a civilian education rather than a garrison one: a circle of people willing to talk about something other than the war just finished, in a country where such talk has become expensive. He arrives a conscript of the victorious army. He leaves unable to go back to being only a musician.
suggested_refs: Zaragoza under Nationalist administration, 1940-1943
sources: Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes, author-authority record

stops.name: Zaragoza, the library of Alfonso Bunuel
stops.date_confidence: within the attested 1940-1943 posting; the individual translations are undated
stops.campa: Alfonso Bunuel, brother of the filmmaker, opens his shelves to the young soldier, and the shelves hold what a garrison town does not stock: surrealist reviews and dream-logic set out as a grammar. Cirlot translates Eluard, Breton, and Artaud here, from borrowed copies, under a regime with no use for any of the three. His surrealism is secondhand from the first day and he never pretends otherwise. No source records the street, the house, or which book came first.
suggested_refs: The library of Alfonso Bunuel in Zaragoza, source of Cirlot's Surrealism

stops.name: Barcelona, back to the ledgers
stops.date_confidence: year attested, summer per the sources; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He comes home in 1943 and returns to the same bank, as though seven years of war on two sides had been unpaid leave. The columns have not changed. He has. The Zaragoza reading rides quietly alongside the arithmetic for five more years, waiting for somewhere public to go, and in the meantime he writes at night: poems, criticism, a diary of an unreasonable sadness begun in a dream. Barcelona under the new order prints little and permits less; the waiting is not idleness but storage.
suggested_refs: The Banco Hispanoamericano, Barcelona, resumed post 1943

stops.name: Barcelona, a cafe on the Ramblas: El libro de Cartago
stops.date_confidence: attested to the last days of 1946; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: In the last days of 1946, at a cafe table on the Ramblas, he writes El libro de Cartago, subtitled Diario de una tristeza irrazonable, out of a dream he had two years earlier. One manuscript goes to Carlos Edmundo de Ory; another copy is illustrated by Julian Gallego early the next year. Both survive. Carthage suits what he is after: a city razed so completely that it survives only in other people's accounts. He will come to handle symbols the same way, at second hand and by comparison.
suggested_refs: El libro de Cartago, manuscript, MACBA collection ref. A13082
sources: MACBA catalogue entry, 'El libro de Cartago'

stops.name: Barcelona, the marriage to Gloria Valenzuela
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August 1947 he marries Gloria Valenzuela. No source names the church; only the date survives. Lourdes is born in 1949 and Victoria in 1955, and the household will hold, in one flat, a clerk's habits, a publisher's deadlines, a growing rack of medieval blades, and a private mythology whose scale nobody outside the family yet suspects. Gloria keeps the last of their houses until her own death in 2008, thirty-five years after his.
suggested_refs: The Cirlot household of Barcelona, 1947-2008

stops.name: Editorial Argos, the bookshop years
stops.date_confidence: sequence attested (after the 1947 marriage, before Gustavo Gili in 1951); the exact years are not recorded
stops.campa: He moves from the bank to the Argos publishing house and bookshop, where books become a livelihood rather than an evening habit. Every account of him gives this two lines at most, unglamorous beside Breton and Tapies. From here on his working day is spent on a page. The sources name the firm and little else: no title, no list he edited, no dates beyond the sequence. The four years at Argos rehearse the twenty-two at Gustavo Gili, and the clerk and the writer stop competing for the same hours.
suggested_refs: Editorial Argos, Barcelona publishing house and bookshop

stops.name: Barcelona, the first issue of Dau al Set
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1948
stops.campa: A hand-printed magazine appears in September 1948, run off Joan-Josep Tharrats's own press: Brossa writing, Tapies and Ponc and Cuixart drawing, Arnau Puig arguing. Dau al Set, the seventh face of the die, the face no throw can show. For a few years it is the only place in Spain where surrealism and its dadaist inheritance speak Catalan in public. Cirlot comes to it from outside, a bank-trained critic with Zaragoza translations in his drawer, and within a year is writing its manifesto.
suggested_refs: Dau al Set, first issue, September 1948, printed by Joan-Josep Tharrats

stops.name: Ateneu Barcelones, the premiere of Preludio
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of October 1948 the hall on Carrer Canuda hears Preludio, his own composition, the single public fruit of eight years under Ardevol. He is thirty-two: still more musician than critic or poet, performing the art he trained in longest and will abandon soonest. No second work of his is ever performed. The same year he joins the Circulo Manuel de Falla, housed by the Institut Francais, and from here on he writes about music rather than making it.
suggested_refs: The Ateneu Barcelones, Carrer Canuda 6, Barcelona
sources: Circulo Manuel de Falla / Institut Francais de Barcelona record

stops.name: Barcelona, the Diccionario de los ismos
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: He publishes a dictionary of the isms: cubism, dadaism, surrealism and their lesser cousins, the movements his own century has thrown off. The same year he publishes a monograph on Stravinsky. Barcelona has lived through most of what the book catalogues, so it is inventory rather than discovery, and the working method is already in place: take a field still in motion, cut it into entries, alphabetize it, and see what the alphabet shows that the chronology hid.
suggested_refs: Diccionario de los ismos (1949) and the monograph Igor Stravinsky (1949)

stops.name: Paris, the Place Blanche and Andre Breton
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Joan Miro makes the introduction, and in a cafe off the Place Blanche, in the Montmartre where the surrealists held their noon meetings, Cirlot shakes the hand of Andre Breton, whom he had translated in a borrowed Zaragoza library while wearing the other side's uniform. Breton invites him into the movement; he declines the membership and keeps the friendship, and is later the only Spanish poet to answer the questionnaire behind L'Art Magique. He dedicates the second Lilith to him, engraved by Tapies and Cuixart.
suggested_refs: The cafes of the Place Blanche, Paris, meeting-ground of Breton's circle

stops.name: Barcelona, the apprenticeship to Marius Schneider
stops.date_confidence: start year attested; most sources end it in 1954, one blogspot source in 1952; the month is conjectural
stops.campa: The German ethnomusicologist Marius Schneider, running the folklore section of the Instituto Espanol de Musicologia in Barcelona, takes him in hand and turns a critic of paintings into a student of symbols. Schneider hears the world as rhythm: mountains and animals and instruments answering each other across traditions on a single common beat. Cirlot takes the method whole, including its refusal to separate what a people believes from what it thinks, and spends five years learning to read correspondence as evidence.
stops.quote: there is no such thing as 'ideas or beliefs', only 'ideas and beliefs'
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, p. xi, citing Marius Schneider approvingly
suggested_refs: Marius Schneider at the Instituto Espanol de Musicologia (CSIC), Barcelona
sources: contradiction: blogspot 'Enigmatico Cirlot I' ends the apprenticeship in 1952

stops.name: Sagrada Familia, Gaudi read as myth
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source records a dated visit; 1950 is the publication year of El arte de Gaudi
stops.campa: El arte de Gaudi appears from Ediciones Omega, and its author reads the unfinished basilica the way he reads a myth: not as engineering but as stone bent into the shape of an idea. No letter or diary places him under the towers on any given day, and the book cannot have been written by a man who never stood there, a few tram stops from every address he keeps in this city. Sixteen years later he returns to the same architect with a whole vocabulary ready for what the stone is doing.
stops.quote: Nothing is meaningless or neutral: everything is significant.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'Analysis of the Symbol,' p. xxxvi
suggested_refs: El arte de Gaudi (Ediciones Omega, Barcelona, 1950)
sources: gap: no attested visit to the site

stops.name: Park Guell, the serpent and the fragment
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: inferred from the subject matter of the Gaudi book; no visit attested and no month recorded
stops.campa: The tiled dragon at the stair, the serpent bench carrying its broken ceramic around the terrace: Gaudi hands him the clearest local examples of a symbolic vocabulary he is only beginning to systematize. Serpent, spiral, colour, fragment. Each becomes an entry later, cross-referenced to India and Egypt and the alchemists, and the Barcelona hillside is named in none of them. No source puts him at the gate on a stated day; the book is the only evidence that he came at all.
stops.quote: Nothing is independent, everything is in some way related to something else.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'Analysis of the Symbol,' p. xxxvi
suggested_refs: Park Guell, Barcelona, and the symbolic vocabulary of Gaudi's ceramics
sources: inferred from El arte de Gaudi
gap: no primary attestation of a visit

stops.name: Barcelona Cathedral, the sword of Pere IV
stops.date_confidence: the Sunday family habit is attested without dates; 1951 is the year the collecting begins
stops.campa: The family goes on Sundays to look at the sword of Pere IV in the cathedral, and out of that habit comes a collection: antique and medieval blades bought and traded across the rest of his life, hung where other men hang pictures. He is not an antiquarian. A sword is the object where his two vocabularies meet, the historical and the symbolic: an edge that cut somebody in a real year, and the vertical line dividing light from dark in every tradition he is reading.
stops.quote: The above considerations make it clear that the symbolic in no way excludes the historical, since both forms may be seen — from the ideological point of view — as functional aspects of a third: the metaphysical principle, the platonic "idea"; or all three may be seen as reciprocal expressions of one meaning on different levels.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'Symbolism and Historicity,' p. xv
suggested_refs: The sword of Pere IV in Barcelona Cathedral; Cirlot's collection of medieval blades
sources: 'El coleccionista de espadas,' Diario de Leon

stops.name: Editorial Gustavo Gili, Carrer del Rossello
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown; the Rossello headquarters is not built until 1954-1960, so his first years sit at an address no source establishes
stops.campa: He joins the publishing house of Gustavo Gili and stays until he dies, twenty-two years of art books made from a desk. The rationalist headquarters on Rossello that later photographs show does not exist yet; it goes up between 1954 and 1960, and where the firm housed him for his first three years is recorded nowhere consulted. From this desk come the criticism, the Gaudi books, and the dictionary, written at night on the same discipline that gets a catalogue to press on time.
suggested_refs: Editorial Gustavo Gili, Carrer del Rossello 87-89, Barcelona (built 1954-1960)
sources: contradiction: employment from 1951 against a building of 1954-1960

stops.name: Sala Caralt, the last exhibition of the group
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1951 (MACBA); the day is not recorded
stops.campa: The Dau al Set painters hang together at the Sala Caralt in October 1951, their second joint exhibition and their last; Cirlot takes part, with Arnau Puig. The group is already dispersing into separate careers, Tapies toward the matter-paintings that will make him famous, Cirlot toward a study nobody in the room would call art criticism. Twelve years later he will cut Tapies off entirely, and no source consulted says why. This is the last room in which they are all still one thing.
suggested_refs: Sala Caralt, Barcelona, October 1951, the second and final Dau al Set group show

stops.name: Vilanova i la Geltru, the Academia del Faro de San Cristobal
stops.date_confidence: membership attested, admission date unknown; 1952 placed inside Eugeni d'Ors's lifetime
stops.campa: Forty-five kilometres down the coast, at the hermitage of Sant Cristofol above the sea, Eugeni d'Ors keeps an academy he founded in 1946 on his own property, half a critics' society and half a private rite. Cirlot is one of its younger men, with Oriol Bohigas and Joan Perucho, in a company presided over by the last great Catalan arbiter of taste. D'Ors dies here in 1954. Fourteen years afterwards Cirlot contributes to the tribute volume published under the academy's name.
suggested_refs: The Ermita de Sant Cristofol, Vilanova i la Geltru, seat of the Academia del Faro de San Cristobal

stops.name: Barcelona, El ojo en la mitologia
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: He publishes a book on a single symbol: the eye in mythology, and what it has meant. It is the dictionary in miniature, the method tested on one entry before being turned loose on a thousand. Gather every tradition's use of the thing, set the uses side by side, let the pattern that survives the comparison stand as the meaning. The comparative habit comes from Schneider, the patience from the ledgers. His own contribution is the confidence that the pattern is really there and not an effect of the arrangement.
suggested_refs: El ojo en la mitologia: su simbolismo (1954)

stops.name: Barcelona, Victoria born on her father's birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia; the article on her father gives 1954, contradicting its own sister page
stops.campa: His second daughter is born on the ninth of April 1955, his own thirty-ninth birthday, the same square on the calendar. She becomes a medievalist, a professor of Romance philology, an editor of Grail literature, and at the end the custodian of everything left on his desk. None of that is visible in 1955. There is a second child in a flat full of blades and page proofs, and a father who has just decided his real subject is not poetry but the structure lying under it.
suggested_refs: Victoria Cirlot, born Barcelona, 9 April 1955

stops.name: Barcelona, the turn recorded in the diagram
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Cirlot's own retrospective periodization, reported at second hand and undated within the year
stops.campa: By his own later account, drawn as a diagram he titles Biografia: Mitologia personal, this is where he turns: away from poetry and surrealism as a practice, toward symbology as a study. Schneider is one cause named on the sheet, Gifreda another. The diagram runs his life in three columns, the work down one side, the family down the other, the vocation through the middle. It is a man drawing his own biography as a symbolic figure, and he is periodizing the life while still inside it.
suggested_refs: 'Biografia: Mitologia personal,' Cirlot's autobiographical diagram
sources: Arsgravis (Universidad de Barcelona), 'Vida-Arte-Simbolo en J. E. Cirlot'

stops.name: Sala Gaspar, the poems read aloud
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the reading is reported without a date; 1955 is placed inside the decade the sources give
stops.campa: In the Consell de Cent gallery that has shown Picasso and Miro he reads unpublished poems aloud: Introduccion, El caballero rojo, the Cuarto canto de la vida muerta. The room is built for hanging pictures rather than for a voice, but postwar Barcelona has few other rooms, and the critic and the poet in him take the same floor on the same evening. The red knight is already riding through the verse, eleven years before the film that will give the rider a woman to ride toward.
suggested_refs: Sala Gaspar, Carrer del Consell de Cent 323, Barcelona
sources: Cristina Zabala Adrada, Las galerias de arte de Barcelona en los anos 40

stops.name: Barcelona, the Diccionario de simbolos tradicionales
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Luis Miracle publishes, in Barcelona, the book that outlasts everything else he writes. A decade of reading done at a publisher's desk by day and a mythographer's desk by night, both in the same flat: alchemy, the Kabbalah, Romanesque capitals, the Vedas, and the archetypes of Carl Jung as the spine holding the comparisons upright. Under the alphabet sits a claim rather than a service: the world is legible entry by entry, and nothing standing in it is inert.
stops.quote: On entering the realms of symbolism, whether by way of systematized artistic forms or the living, dynamic forms of dreams and visions, we have constantly kept in mind the essential need to mark out the field of symbolic action, in order to prevent confusion between phenomena which might appear to be identical when they are merely similar or externally related.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'Delimitation of the Symbolic,' p. xi
suggested_refs: Diccionario de simbolos tradicionales, Luis Miracle, Barcelona, 1958

segments.name: The Book Travels, the Man Does Not

stops.name: Cuenca, the museum built by letter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the correspondence is undated in the sources and no source places him in Cuenca
stops.campa: In the hanging houses over the Huecar gorge, Fernando Zobel is assembling a museum for Spanish abstraction. Cirlot never comes. He sends letters instead, intense and continuous, which encourage the idea and shape it, together with a monograph on Gustavo Torner, one of the painters who will hang there. He works on the room from a Barcelona desk, by envelope, four hundred kilometres away, and sees it finished only in photographs. Nothing consulted places him in Cuenca on any day.
suggested_refs: Museo de Arte Abstracto Espanol, Casas Colgadas, Cuenca
sources: gap: no source attests his physical presence in Cuenca

stops.name: London, A Dictionary of Symbols
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Routledge and Kegan Paul publish Jack Sage's translation with a foreword by Herbert Read, and the book leaves Spanish. Read, who knows him, sets down the plain facts for an English reader and calls him the leading theoretician of the Barcelona group. Philosophical Library issues it in New York the same year. From this edition the dictionary travels on into Hebrew and Portuguese, into art schools and film sets and the hands of readers who never learn that its author kept a clerk's hours.
stops.quote: Juan Eduardo Cirlot was born in Barcelona in 1916, and after matriculating from the College of the Jesuits there, studied music. From 1943 onwards he was active as a poet, and published four volumes of verse between 1946 and 1953.
stops.quote_source: Herbert Read, Foreword to Cirlot's A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed. (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1971), p. ix
suggested_refs: A Dictionary of Symbols, trans. Jack Sage, Routledge and Kegan Paul, London, 1962

stops.name: Barcelona, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Juan Cirlot dies in 1962, eleven years before his son. No source consulted records the illness, the funeral, or the burial place, and the son who is at this moment the most systematic reader of death symbolism in Spain leaves no published word about it. The fact survives as a bare date in a chronology otherwise crowded with print runs and deadlines. The record of the year holds two things: a translation published in London, and a grave in Barcelona that nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: Gap: no burial record located for Juan Cirlot the elder

stops.name: Barcelona, the break with Tapies
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, and no source gives a cause
stops.campa: In 1963 he severs ties with Antoni Tapies. They had shared a magazine, a gallery, a manifesto, and fifteen years of the city's postwar art, and Tapies had cut engravings for his Lilith. No source consulted gives a reason and neither man appears to have published one. The break is recorded as a fact and stays a fact. From here his public life narrows steadily toward the private material, and the friendships that survive are mostly conducted by letter.
suggested_refs: Gap: no source states the cause of the 1963 rupture with Tapies

stops.name: Barcelona, a cinema and The War Lord
stops.date_confidence: 1966 per en. and es.wikipedia, dating the Spanish release; Villena instead ties the encounter to the film's US release of November 1965
stops.campa: In a Barcelona cinema whose name nobody recorded he watches Franklin Schaffner's The War Lord, and then watches it again, and keeps going back. Rosemary Forsyth rises out of the swamp water as Bronwyn, a village girl in an eleventh-century Frisian marsh, and he calls her Celtic because that is the country he needs her to come from. He is fifty, and has spent thirty years cataloguing other people's symbols. This one has a face, and it will not stay inside the dictionary.
suggested_refs: The War Lord (dir. Franklin Schaffner, 1965), Spanish release El senor de la guerra
sources: contradiction: Luis Antonio de Villena dates the viewing to 1965

stops.name: Barcelona, the Bronwyn cycle opens
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: The first Bronwyn is published and a cycle begins that runs to sixteen books. Across them she becomes the Grail, Christ, Ophelia, the Shekhinah, matter, Venus, the universe; the poet becomes a knight of the High Middle Ages who dies of a lance wound, loved by a woman he cannot reach. The form is older than the film. Jaufre Rudel sang amor de lonh, love for a woman never seen, eight centuries earlier. Cirlot fills the inherited shape with a face from a Barcelona screen and works it in permutations, the letters of the name rearranged until they yield.
stops.quote: not only do all dragons stand for The Dragon, but any symbolic daub resembling a dragon is also The Dragon
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'The Common Rhythm of Schneider,' p. xxxiv
suggested_refs: The Bronwyn cycle, 1967-1971, sixteen books
sources: Medievalia (UAB) scholarship on the Bronwyn cycle

stops.name: Toledo, the order that is not his
stops.date_confidence: gap: no source consulted places Cirlot in Toledo at any date, or links him to any order of that name; the date marks only where the question falls in his life
stops.campa: There is an Orden de Toledo. Luis Bunuel founded it on San Jose's day in 1923, naming himself condestable, with Pepin Bello as secretary and Lorca and Alberti and Dali among the caballeros, and it ran until the war closed everything down. Cirlot's one thread to that company is Luis's brother Alfonso, whose Zaragoza shelves handed him surrealism in 1941. No document joins him to the order itself. The chivalry he actually holds is unaffiliated and one man's, written in Barcelona in these years: knight, lady, lance, and no chapter house at all.
suggested_refs: La Orden de Toledo, founded 1923 by Luis Bunuel; no documented link to Cirlot
sources: A*Desk, 'The Order of Toledo: Bunuel and the occult versus the hegemonic'
gap: no source connects Cirlot to any Order of Toledo

stops.name: Barcelona, Del no mundo and the dictionary enlarged
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: In one year he publishes a book of aphorisms called Del no mundo and enlarges the dictionary for its second Spanish edition, adding entries, among them phonetic symbolism: the claim that a sound carries meaning before a word means anything. The English second edition follows in 1971. The two books belong together. One says the world is not the world; the other goes on patiently indexing it, on the working assumption that every part of it stands for something and the standing-for can be written down.
suggested_refs: Del no mundo: Aforismos (1969); second Spanish edition of the Diccionario (1969)

stops.name: Madrid, the essay in Cuadernos Hispanoamericanos
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; whether he came to Madrid to speak it, as some accounts suggest of a 1969 talk, is unsettled
stops.campa: Cuadernos Hispanoamericanos, published from the Instituto de Cultura Hispanica, prints Bronwyn: simbolismo de un argumento cinematografico, the theoretical spine of a cycle already many books deep. Here he does to his own obsession what he did to alchemy and the Romanesque, taking the argument of a film he cannot stop watching and reading it as a symbolic structure. Whether he stood in Madrid to say it aloud or posted it from Barcelona is not settled by anything consulted.
suggested_refs: 'Bronwyn (Simbolismo de un argumento cinematografico),' Cuadernos Hispanoamericanos, July 1970
sources: Los papeles de Don Cogito, reproducing the 1970 text

stops.name: Barcelona, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown
stops.campa: Pancreatic cancer, 1971. The cycle is unfinished, the dictionary is made and selling in three languages, Victoria is sixteen. Two years remain and the sources give nothing of their daily texture: no hospital, no treatment, no letters. The man who wrote that the labyrinth and the pilgrimage both point at one centre goes on working. In his poems he has already chosen the death he wants, a lance in the side in an eleventh-century field, and the death arriving is an ordinary tumour in an ordinary city.
stops.quote: The idea of the world as a labyrinth or of life as a pilgrimage leads to the idea of the "centre" as a symbol of the absolute goal of Man — Paradise regained, heavenly Jerusalem.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, 'The Symbolism of Alchemy,' p. xxvii
suggested_refs: Gap: no record of hospital or treatment, 1971-1973

stops.name: Carrer d'Hercegovina, the surgery and the same day
stops.date_confidence: attested; the street appears as Hercegovina in some sources and Herzegovino in others
stops.campa: On the eleventh of May 1973 he is operated on and dies that same day, at home, on a Barcelona street named for a country he never saw. He is fifty-seven. Gloria keeps the house another thirty-five years; when she dies in 2008 the daughters finally empty it, and the archive comes out: manuscripts, the diagrams, the correspondence, the swords. The birth address in the Eixample was never written down. The death address is a few kilometres uphill, and it was.
suggested_refs: The Cirlot house on Carrer d'Hercegovina, Barcelona, emptied in 2008

stops.name: Barcelona, the grave that no register holds
stops.date_confidence: gap: no cemetery record for Cirlot was found in any source consulted; the date is the day after the death, not an attested burial date
stops.campa: Where he is buried is not recorded in anything reachable. Montjuic holds a great many of his contemporaries, and no listing found ties his name to a plot there or anywhere else; the searches come back empty. No plaque marks the birth house, no street carries his name, no monument stands anywhere in the city. The man who wrote out what every stone on every grave has meant to every tradition leaves, in his own town, an address for the death and none at all for the burial.
suggested_refs: Gap: Cementiris de Barcelona records return no entry for Cirlot
sources: gap: searches of Montjuic and Sant Gervasi records returned nothing
gap: no commemorative plaque or monument located

stops.name: Valencia, Mundo de Juan Eduardo Cirlot
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exhibition ran to 17 November 1996
stops.campa: The IVAM hangs him for two months: some ninety works by the surrealists, the Dau al Set painters, the informalists and abstract expressionists he wrote for, arranged as the world one critic saw, with his poetry and his music in the cases between. Twenty-three years dead, he hangs on a public wall as a way of looking rather than as an author. It is the first time an institution treats the criticism, the poems, and the dictionary as one body of work instead of three careers.
suggested_refs: IVAM, 'Mundo de Juan Eduardo Cirlot,' 19 September to 17 November 1996

stops.name: Madrid, Siruela keeps it in print
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the continuous print run since 1997 is stated by the publisher's own catalogue and not independently checked
stops.campa: Editorial Siruela takes the Diccionario de simbolos and does not let it go out of print: some twenty printings, a tenth edition by 2003, a book that has outlived its first publisher and most of the movements its author catalogued. It sits in Spanish bookshops beside popular reference and is read by painters, novelists, film designers, and adolescents, few of whom know that it was assembled at night by a man who spent his days making other people's art books.
suggested_refs: Editorial Siruela, Diccionario de simbolos, in print since 1997

stops.name: Barcelona, El libro de Cartago comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 2016, the centenary year of his birth; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: A hundred years after the birth in the Eixample, Vaso Roto issues El libro de Cartago in facsimile, five hundred copies prepared and signed by Victoria Cirlot, reproducing both surviving versions: the manuscript he sent to Carlos Edmundo de Ory and the copy Julian Gallego illustrated in 1947. The original stays at the MACBA under a catalogue number. The diary of an unreasonable sadness, written at a cafe table in a defeated city, comes back as an object made to be kept.
suggested_refs: El libro de Cartago, facsimile, Vaso Roto Ediciones, September 2016, 500 copies

stops.name: New York, the revised dictionary
stops.date_confidence: attested by the NYRB product page; retail listings give 2022
stops.campa: New York Review Books reissues A Dictionary of Symbols revised and expanded: Jack Sage's translation carried forward, new translation by Valerie Miles, Herbert Read's foreword still standing in front of it, and an afterword by the daughter born on her father's birthday. The book has now been in print in English for close to sixty years. Its author's grave is still unlocated, and the entries go on being consulted by readers who never learn his name.
stops.quote: The temptation to over-substantiate an argument is one which is difficult to resist.
stops.quote_source: Juan Eduardo Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, 2nd ed., trans. Jack Sage, Introduction, p. xi
